name: Approval inbox
description: The screen an approver lives in: everything waiting on their signature in one queue, the record beside it, and the decision on a rail where the hand already is. Deciding removes the record from the queue and lands the user on the next one without a reload.
when_to_use: The screen an approver works in — purchase orders above a buyer's limit, goods receipts short against the challan, rate contracts, credit notes — worked one after another until the queue is empty. The boundary that decides most screens is the one against list-detail, and it is the difference between reading a queue and deciding one. list-detail is right when the queue is read: the selection moves, the detail follows, and nothing is written; its qc-hold variant is a work-one-at-a-time queue and it is the model this entry is built on, so take that one whenever the screen has no write on it. Reach for this the moment a decision is taken on the record, because a decision drags behind it the whole apparatus list-detail deliberately has none of: an action rail with the decision on it, a reason required before a refusal can be sent, the record leaving the queue when it is acted on, an in-flight state and a refusal from the server, an approval limit that can put a record beyond this user entirely, delegation, and a queue whose length changes under the user while they are looking at it. Against index-page: that is the register — every record of a kind, sorted, filtered, searched — and it is where somebody goes to find one specific order rather than to work through all of them. An approver asking what happened to PO-2026-0418 last March goes to the register; an approver clearing today's work comes here, and the two are different screens even when they list the same rows. Against alert-dialog: that is a component this screen uses rather than a screen of its own — the reason a rejection asks for, the confirmation a bulk approval takes, the refusal the server sends back — and it is composed into this layout rather than redrawn inside it. A screen that creates or edits one of these records is form-page.
rules: This renders inside app-shell, in its main column. The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[660px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box, and the confirmation dialogs are absolute inset-0 against that frame. As a real page: drop the wrapper height and border, put h-screen overflow-hidden on <body>, and make the dialogs fixed inset-0.

Act and advance is the whole component and everything else follows from it. The user reads, decides, and lands on the next record without a reload and without going back to a list. That means four things have to be decided together and none of them can be left to the browser: where focus goes when the record under it stops existing, what the live region says, what happens to the item that was just acted on, and what the screen does when the queue empties under the user's hands.

Focus lands on the record region, not back on the queue and not on the button that was pressed. Leaving it on the button is the tempting answer — the rail survives the swap, so Approve is still under the finger and the next approval is one Enter away — and it is exactly why it is wrong: a held Enter approves four orders nobody read, and these are signatures. Sending it back to the queue option is no better, because the keyboard user then has to walk the whole record again to reach the decision. Focus goes to the detail region, whose accessible name is the record heading, so the new record is announced by the mechanism that already exists and there is deliberately one Tab between the user and the next Approve.

Focus announces which record is now open; the live region announces what happened to the last one. Those are two different sentences and only one of them is deliverable by focus, which is why this layout has both and why they must not overlap. The region says the outcome and the count — "PO-2026-0418 approved. 6 left in your inbox" — and never repeats the record name that the focus move is already reading out.

Nothing is optimistic. An approval is a server write with legal weight, so the row does not leave the queue and the pill does not change until the server has said it committed. Drawing Approved on the click and reconciling afterwards means a screen that has told a plant head they signed something they did not, and there is no toast that unsays it. While the write is in flight the record stays exactly where it is, the rail goes aria-busy, the pressed button keeps its width and says what it is doing, and the other decisions on that record are disabled — the queue itself stays live, because taking the arrow keys away for the length of a slow request is taking the session away.

A refusal is said where the record is, and where the record is depends on the refusal. If the order is still in front of the user — it was amended under them, a budget check failed — the refusal belongs on that record, above the rail. If the order has already left their inbox because somebody else approved it first, there is no record left to hang it on, so it goes into a page-level alert strip under the header and stays until it is dismissed. Both say whether anything was written, because "it failed" and "it failed and nothing was written" are different facts and only one of them is safe to press again.

A refusal needs a reason and that is why it cannot be optimistic in any form. The reason is part of the write, not a note attached afterwards: a rejection with no reason returns the order to a buyer who has nothing to change, and a screen that removes the row on the click and then finds the reason field empty has already lied to the queue. Reject opens alert-dialog's reason shape — one required field, the confirm genuinely disabled until it is filled — and the row leaves only when the POST carrying that reason has come back.

An item above this user's limit has no Approve button at all. A greyed-out one with no explanation is the most-reported fault in every internal application there has ever been, and aria-disabled with a described reason is only the right answer where the user could plausibly clear the condition. Nobody clears their own approval limit, so the honest rail says what the limit is, what the order is worth, who it goes to instead, and offers escalation as its primary — the action that is actually available is the one on the rail.

Delegation is a property of the session, not a choice made per record, so it is stated once in a strip under the page header and repeated in the verb on the button — "Approve as Nilesh Patil". The limit travels with the authority rather than with the person: a delegate approving for a plant head approves up to the plant head's limit, not their own, and the rail says whose limit is in force. What is written is both names, because an audit that records only the delegate cannot answer who was accountable and one that records only the principal cannot answer who was at the keyboard.

Bulk approval is offered by the screen, never assembled by ticking rows in the queue. The queue is a listbox and a listbox is one Tab stop, so a checkbox inside an option is unreachable — that is list-detail's rule and it holds here. It is also the better design: the server is what knows which items are alike, so the offer is made from the record the user is already reading — same vendor, same rate contract, all inside the limit — and the confirmation dialog is where the checkboxes are legal and where one can be dropped. Anything that needs a reason, anything above the limit and anything amended since the queue was drawn is named as excluded rather than quietly left out.

The queue is heterogeneous and the record pane is not one template. Four document kinds arrive in one inbox and they do not share a shape, so the pane draws the record's own list of facts and its own line columns, and what stays constant is the header, the approval trail and the rail. A pane hard-coded to purchase orders is a pane that renders a credit note with four empty cells.

Every item in this queue carries the Approved pill and the amber dot, which reads backwards for one second and is correct: in this system Approved is the waiting-on-someone state, not a decision that has been taken. The pill that changes is Overdue, on anything past the approval service level, and it is the one thing in the queue that is allowed to be red. list-detail's requisition queue makes the same choice, and following it matters more than the reading.

No single-key shortcuts on any decision. A screen this keyboard-driven invites them, and an approval fired by a stray A is a signature nobody meant to give. The decisions are ordinary Tab stops on a rail the user reaches after committing to a record.

The age that matters is the age with this approver, not the age of the document. An order raised three weeks ago and forwarded this morning is one day old on this screen, and writing the document date there is how a queue acquires a column of alarming numbers that nobody can act on.

anatomy.description: The fixed-height flex column holding everything. The page does not scroll; the three regions inside it do.
shrink-0. page-header's block reduced to what an inbox needs: the one h1, and under it a role="status" count line saying how many are waiting, what they are worth and how old the oldest is.
Present only while the user is acting for somebody else. A neutral alert card under the header saying whose authority is in force and until when, with the way out of it.
The list pane. A 320–352px column at md and up, full width below it, holding the listbox and its own header with the count and the kind filter.
li role="option" with a roving tabindex: the status dot, the document number, the value, the kind and party, and how long it has been with this approver. Nothing focusable inside it.
A section labelled by the record heading, tabindex="-1" so a decision can put focus on it. Header and trail are shrink-0; only the body between them scrolls.

An aside carrying the decision. A 288px column at lg and up, a bar across the foot of the record below it — one element, not two copies. It holds the limit position, the approval trail and the decision buttons, and it never scrolls out of reach.
A role="alert" region above the rail's buttons, in the document from first paint and empty, for a server that refused a write on the record still on screen.
A second role="alert" under the page header, for a refusal about a record that has already left the queue and has nowhere else to be said.
One role="status" on the frame, present at first paint, carrying the outcome of each decision and the size of what is left.

behaviour: Up and Down walk the queue, Home and End go to its ends, and the ends clamp rather than wrap. Enter commits and moves focus into the record. The arrow keys are bound on the listbox, never on the window, so the kind filter and any search above the list keep their own caret keys.
A decision is a request. The record stays in the queue and the rail goes aria-busy until the server answers; nothing about the record changes on the click.

When the server commits, the record leaves the queue, the counts rewrite, the selection moves to the record that took its place, the record body scrolls back to its top, and focus lands on the record region so its name is read.
The live region says what was decided and how many are left. It does not name the record that is now open, because the focus move is already reading that out.

When the server refuses, nothing leaves the queue unless the refusal is that the record has already gone. A refusal about a record on screen is drawn above the rail; a refusal about a record that has left is drawn under the page header and waits to be dismissed.
A refusal requires a reason before it can be sent, and the reason is collected in an alert dialog whose confirm is disabled until the field is answered.

An item above the user's approval limit is fully readable and has no approve action at all. The rail offers escalation instead, and escalating removes it from this inbox and puts it in the approver's.

Bulk approval is offered from the record the user is on, over the items the server has grouped with it. The confirmation lists every item with a checkbox and lists what was excluded and why; the whole set is one write and one outcome.
The last decision in the queue collapses the screen to the cleared state rather than leaving two empty panes. The cleared state states what was done, over what scope, and that nothing is filtered.

Below md the queue and the record are two screens. Opening a record shows it with the decision bar pinned at the foot, so the decision is reachable without scrolling past the record; Back and Escape return to the queue with focus on the option that was opened.
accessibility: One main, one h1, and the regions under it are h2s: the queue and the record. The record heading is what aria-labelledby points at, so the region name changes with the selection and a decision that moves focus there announces the new record.

The queue is a listbox named by its heading, one option carrying aria-selected="true" and every other carrying aria-selected="false". Exactly one option holds tabindex="0" and it moves with the selection, so tabbing out to the rail and back returns to the record being decided.

No option contains a button, a link or a checkbox. A listbox is one Tab stop and a control inside an option cannot be reached; the decisions live on the rail, on a record the user has already committed to.

The action rail is an <aside> with an accessible name so it can be found and skipped in a landmark list. It is one element that changes shape at lg, not two copies behind media queries — two copies mean two sets of ids and a decision posted from the one nobody could see.
The role="status" on the frame exists before anything changes and carries only what focus does not deliver: the outcome of the decision and the size of what is left.

Both refusal regions carry role="alert" and are in the DOM empty from first paint. A region created in the same frame as its first message counts as content that was always there and is announced to nobody, which is the failure that costs most in exactly this case.

A decision in flight sets aria-busy on the rail and keeps the pressed button focused, enabled and the same width. Disabling the control that was just pressed moves focus to the body, and the keyboard user who approved an order is then at the top of the document.

Where there is no approve action the button is absent rather than disabled, and the reason is ordinary text in the rail. A disabled button cannot be focused or described, so the explanation attached to one reaches nobody.
The status dot on an option is aria-hidden and the state is a word in the option text, so the queue is readable without colour.
No decision carries a single-key shortcut, and none of them is the first focusable thing on the page.

approvals/views.py @require_POST def approve(request, pk): doc = get_object_or_404(Document.awaiting(request.user), pk=pk) try: doc.approve(by=request.user, on_behalf_of=request.delegation) except AlreadyDecided as e: said = f"{doc.number} was approved by {e.by} at {e.at:%H:%M}, before " said += "your approval reached the server. Nothing was written by you." except Stale: said = f"{doc.number} changed while it was on screen. Nothing was written." else: said = f"{doc.number} approved." queue = list(Document.awaiting(request.user)) said += f" {len(queue)} left in your inbox." response = render(request, "approvals/_inbox.html", inbox_context(request, queue)) response["HX-Trigger"] = json.dumps({"decided": said}) return response Document.awaiting(user) is the whole routing rule in one place — the user's own queue plus anything they hold a live delegation for — and it is re-run on every response, so the queue and the record can never disagree about what is left. It is also what the POST re-checks: a document that has left the queue between the render and the click is not in the queryset, so the 404 is the concurrency guard rather than something bolted on beside it. within_limit and next_approver come off the model against the authority in force, which is the delegation limit when one is being used and the user's own otherwise. The template never compares two figures itself — a limit worked out in a template is a limit that will be worked out differently in the next template. status_dot_class is one of the five locked values — bg-zinc-500, bg-amber-500, bg-red-600, bg-emerald-600, bg-zinc-400 — so the pill shape is written once here and only the dot changes. {% endcomment %}
